sections.text: # Sedimentary Rocks — Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text: **Bridge — sedimentary stratigraphy as a version control log:** Each stratum is a commit: it records environmental state at a moment in time (grain size = energy, fossils = biota, chemistry = ocean composition), and the layer order gives a deterministic sequence. Unconformities are missing commits — either the record was never written (non-deposition) or was deleted (erosion); they are the geological equivalent of a `git rebase` that dropped commits, leaving the index and the log inconsistent. Angular unconformities are especially legible: the underlying strata were tilted (a branch diverged), eroded (commits overwritten), then new horizontal strata deposited on top (main branch continued). Fossils are tagged releases: index fossils with short stratigraphic ranges are version tags with precise timestamps, enabling correlation of the same "release" across widely separated outcrops. Lateral facies changes are the same feature behaving differently in different environments — same commit timestamp, different local state.

sections.text: ## The Big Picture

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text: Sedimentary rocks cover ~75% of Earth's land surface but are only ~5% of the crust by volume (a thin veneer). They matter disproportionately because they contain: the fossil record, petroleum systems, groundwater aquifers, most economically mined coal, and the chemical evidence of past climates.

sections.text: ## Weathering — Breaking Down Source Rock

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text:
### Physical (Mechanical) Weathering
- **Freeze-thaw** — water in cracks expands 9% on freezing → fractures rock
- **Pressure unloading (exfoliation)** — granite batholiths exposed by erosion → confining pressure removed → sheets spall off (Half Dome, Yosemite)
- **Abrasion** — river/glacier grinding; produces increasingly rounded, sorted particles
- **Thermal expansion** — day/night cycles crack desert rocks

sections.text: **Weathering stability (field observation rule):** Bowen's series reversed = weathering resistance sequence. Quartz (last to crystallize) is most stable; olivine (first to crystallize) weathers first.

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text:
```
NAME         DIAMETER     SORTING     ROCK NAME
-----------  -----------  ----------  ------------------
Boulders     >256 mm      —           Conglomerate (rounded)
Cobbles      64–256 mm                Breccia (angular)
Pebbles      4–64 mm                  (gravel → conglomerate)
Granules     2–4 mm
Sand         0.063–2 mm   Good        Sandstone
             (0.25–0.5mm              (quartz dominant in mature)
              = medium)
Silt         0.004–0.063  Moderate    Siltstone / Loess
Clay         <0.004 mm    Any         Mudstone / Shale
                                      (most common sedimentary rock)
```

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text:
**Rounding and sorting as transport indicators:**
- Angular, poorly sorted → short transport (glacial till, rockfall)
- Rounded, well-sorted → long transport (eolian dune sand, beach sand)
- Rounding of quartz requires much more energy than rounding of feldspar

sections.text: ## Chemical and Biogenic Sedimentary Rocks

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text:
| Rock | Origin | Composition | Environment |
|------|--------|-------------|-------------|
| Limestone | Biochemical + chemical | CaCO₃ | Shallow warm marine |
| Chalk | Biogenic (coccoliths) | CaCO₃ | Pelagic (open ocean) |
| Dolomite | Diagenetic replacement | CaMg(CO₃)₂ | Restricted marine/burial |
| Chert | Biochemical (radiolaria/diatoms) | SiO₂ | Deep ocean, or hot spring |
| Rock salt (halite) | Evaporite | NaCl | Restricted basin evaporation |
| Gypsum | Evaporite | CaSO₄·2H₂O | Evaporite sequence |
| Coal | Biochemical | Organic carbon | Swamp/peat environment |
| Iron formation (BIF) | Chemical | Fe₂O₃/SiO₂ | Pre-2.5 Ga ocean (Proterozoic) |
| Phosphorite | Biochemical | Ca₅(PO₄)₃ | Upwelling zones |

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text:
**Evaporite sequence** — precipitation order as seawater evaporates (decreasing solubility):
CaCO₃ (calcite) → CaSO₄ (gypsum) → NaCl (halite) → KCl → MgSO₄

sections.text: **Facies** = a body of rock with distinct characteristics (lithology + fossils) deposited in a specific environment. Facies change laterally (facies belts) and vertically (facies sequences reflecting sea-level change).

```
BURIAL DEPTH    PROCESS              RESULT
------------    ------------------   ----------------------------
0–1 km          Compaction           Clay porosity: 80% → 30%
                Dewatering           Pore water expelled
                                     Soft sediment deformation

sections.text:
1–3 km          Cementation          Pore space filled by
                                     precipitated minerals
                                     (calcite, silica, iron oxide)

                                     dissolve at contacts

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text:
```
**Common cements and their implications:**
- **Calcite cement** — formed from marine pore water; limestones, some sandstones
- **Silica cement** — produces very hard, tough quartzite-like sandstones
- **Iron oxide cement** — red/brown staining in "red beds" (oxidizing conditions)
- **Pyrite framboids** — reducing (anoxic) burial conditions

sections.text: ## Decision Cheat Sheet

metadata.title: Sedimentary Rocks - Stratigraphy, Steno, Depositional Environments

sections.text:
| Field / Basin Question | Use This Diagnostic | Likely Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| What was the transport energy? | Grain size | Gravel/sand = high energy; silt/clay = low energy or quiet-water settling |
| How far did sediment travel? | Rounding + sorting + mineral maturity | Rounded, well-sorted quartz sand = long reworking; angular, mixed clasts = short transport |
| Is this river, beach, desert, or deep marine? | Sedimentary structures + fossils | Cross-beds, ripples, graded beds, mud cracks, and fossil assemblages constrain environment |
| Is this a time marker or environment marker? | Fossils vs facies | Index fossils correlate age; facies diagnose depositional setting |
| Is a gap present in the record? | Unconformity geometry | Angular, erosional, or nonconformity surfaces mark missing time |
| Is it a carbonate system? | HCl reaction + fossils + texture | Limestone reacts strongly; dolomite weakly unless powdered; fossils imply biogenic carbonate |
| Is it an evaporite? | Crystal habit + basin context | Halite/gypsum imply restricted evaporation; do not rely on taste as a primary test |
| Could it be a reservoir rock? | Porosity + permeability + seal/source context | Sandstones and carbonates can store fluids only if pore network and trap timing work |
| Could it be a source rock? | Organic richness + anoxic laminations + maturity | Dark shale or carbonate mud can generate hydrocarbons only inside the thermal window |
